title: Logistic Regression
interviewAnswer: Logistic regression models log-odds as a linear function of features and maps them through a sigmoid to a probability. Training usually minimizes log loss rather than MSE.
why: It is one of the best interview algorithms because it combines linear models, probability, classification, loss functions and interpretability.
intuition: The model computes a linear score and passes it through a sigmoid so the output lies between 0 and 1. A threshold then converts probability into a class.
deepDive: Logistic regression models log-odds linearly. It is typically trained with binary cross-entropy / negative log likelihood. Coefficients describe additive changes in log-odds per unit feature change, conditional on the other features.
code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced')
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
proba = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:,1]
commonMistakes: Calling it a regression model because of the name without explaining classification.
Assuming 0.5 is always the right threshold.
followUps: Why use log loss instead of MSE?
How do coefficients map to odds ratios?
production: It is often a superb baseline because it trains fast, is easy to calibrate/interpret and exposes whether more complex models are truly necessary.
workedExample: In rare-failure prediction, fit probabilities, evaluate PR metrics and choose a threshold from the false-negative/false-positive cost rather than default 0.5.

lab.goal: Build binary logistic regression and verify probabilities/decision boundary.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(1)
X=rng.normal(size=(300,2)); y=(X[:,0]+.7*X[:,1]>0).astype(float)
Xb=np.c_[np.ones(len(X)),X]; w=np.zeros(3)
def sigmoid(z): return 1/(1+np.exp(-z))
for _ in range(2000):
    p=sigmoid(Xb@w)
    w-=0.1*(Xb.T@(p-y)/len(y))
print('accuracy',((sigmoid(Xb@w)>=.5)==y).mean())
